A remedy is anything — a medicine, an action, or a solution — that fixes, cures, or corrects something that is wrong, harmful, or painful.

Think of it this way: whenever something has gone wrong — a sickness, a bad situation, or an injustice — a remedy is what makes it better or right again. The word always carries the idea of correction. Something broken was there, and the remedy is what addresses it.

1. In Health and Medicine

This is the most familiar use. In health, a remedy is a treatment or medicine that heals an illness, relieves pain, or removes a physical problem.

"Ginger tea is a popular home remedy for nausea." "The doctor found a remedy for her skin condition."

Notice the phrase home remedy in the first example. This is an extremely common expression. A home remedy is a simple, traditional, or natural treatment you prepare at home — without a doctor's prescription — to treat a minor illness. Examples include honey and lemon for a sore throat, aloe vera gel for a sunburn, or steam inhalation for a blocked nose. These are passed down through generations and are part of everyday life in most cultures.

2. For General Problems and Bad Situations

Remedy is also used more broadly to mean any solution or corrective action that fixes a difficult or unpleasant situation — not just a medical one.

"Rest and music were her remedy for stress." "The city's remedy for traffic was to build a new road." "Laughter is often the best remedy for a bad mood."

In this sense, the word carries the feeling of relief and restoration — something that takes a bad thing and moves it toward being better.

3. In Law

In legal language, a remedy is the means by which a court corrects a legal wrong. When someone has been harmed because of another person's unlawful or unfair action, the court provides a remedy to make things right again.

Legal remedies usually take one of two forms. The first is monetary — the wrongdoer is ordered to pay money to the person who was harmed. This is called "damages." The second is non-monetary — for example, a court may order someone to stop doing something harmful (this is called an "injunction"), or order them to fulfill the terms of a contract they broke (called "specific performance").

"The judge awarded a legal remedy to the victims of the fraud." "The only remedy available to her was to sue for damages."

A remedy addresses the problem, not just the surface.
The true spirit of the word "remedy" is something that gets to the root of what's wrong and corrects it. This is subtly different from "relief," which only temporarily eases discomfort without solving the underlying problem. Pain medication might bring relief; surgery might be the remedy. The word remedy implies a more meaningful, corrective action.

A remedy doesn't guarantee a perfect or complete cure.
In everyday use, calling something a remedy doesn't mean it will work perfectly or instantly. It simply means something designed or intended to correct the problem. Some remedies work fully, some partially, and some not at all — but the intent behind the word is always to fix.

A remedy is always tied to a specific problem.
A remedy never exists in isolation. It always exists for something — a remedy for a cold, a remedy for injustice, a remedy for loneliness. This is why you will almost always see the word followed by "for." If someone says "We need a remedy," your natural follow-up question would be, "A remedy for what?"

Home remedy — a simple, traditional treatment made at home for minor ailments, not prescribed by a doctor.

Legal remedy — a court-ordered solution to correct a legal wrong.

Remedy for [something] — the standard way the word is used: a remedy for a problem.

"There is no remedy" — means there is no solution or fix available for the situation.

"Seek a remedy" — to look for a solution, most commonly used in legal or formal contexts.

"Beyond remedy" — a situation so bad or so far gone that nothing can fix it. Similar to "beyond repair."
A Final Way to Remember It

If you want one clear mental image to anchor this word: imagine something broken — a sick body, a broken relationship, a legal injustice. Now imagine something that comes in and sets it right. That thing is the remedy. It is always a response to something wrong. It is always aimed at correction and restoration. Whether it's a cup of herbal tea or a court order, the word "remedy" points to the thing that steps in to make things better.
